lesson.title: Build a report you can defend

lead.text: Here is the sales report. Each row is one order, with an id, the shop that sold it, the units, the price of one unit and a flag that says whether the customer has paid. Before you add any column up, it helps to ask what a single row stands for. That is called the grain of the table. Here the grain is one order, and the id is what tells one order from another.

If every row is one order, no id should appear twice. A repeated id would mean the same order was entered on two rows, and any total would count it twice. The method duplicated() checks for this. It marks a row True when its value has already appeared higher up the column, so the first time an id turns up it is False and each repeat after it is True. Summing the Trues gives the number of extra rows. The figure runs the check on the order ids and then on the shop names.

afterFigure.text: The ids give 0, so every row is its own order and the table has 5 rows. The shop names give 2, because Bay and Hill each appear twice. That is no fault, since a shop sells many orders. A repeated id would be a fault. The check means something only on the column that identifies each row.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Lake', 'Hill'], 'units': [2, 3, 4, 1, 2], 'price': [5, 8, None, 6, 8], 'paid': [True, True, True, False, True]})
duplicate_ids = orders['id'].duplicated().sum()
rows = len(orders)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Lake', 'Hill'], 'units': [2, 3, 4, 1, 2], 'price': [5, 8, None, 6, 8], 'paid': [True, True, True, False, True]})
repeated_shops = orders['shop'].duplicated().sum()

lead.text: Run the same check by hand on a shorter list of ids. Work out which rows count as repeats, and which row is the first of its kind.

reveal.text: You counted the repeats, not every row that shares an id. Only the later occurrences are flagged, which is the number of orders counted twice.

lead.text: Once you know a row is an order, the next decision is which orders belong in the report. This report is about money that has come in, so only orders marked as paid count. Those orders make up the population of the report, and the paid column is how you pick them out.

In the table, orders 1, 2, 3 and 5 are paid, and order 4, from Lake, is not. Filtering with orders[orders['paid']] keeps the four paid rows and leaves the fifth out. You met filters like this earlier. What matters here is the order of the work. Decide who counts first and add up afterwards. If you total all five orders and call the result paid revenue, the unpaid order sits inside the number where nobody can see it.

steps.headline: Paid flags are True, False, True and True. How many orders belong in the paid report?

workedSteps.text: The paid flag decides who counts. How many flags are True?
The rest are left out. How many orders is that?

lead.text: Among the four paid orders, one has a gap. Order 3 has units but no price, so its price is missing. Revenue is units times price, which makes order 3's revenue missing as well. The other three are known: order 1 earned £10, order 2 earned £24 and order 5 earned £16.

There are two tempting ways to hide the gap. Filling it with a zero claims that order 3 earned nothing, and the data does not say that. Reporting the total as if it were complete is the other. The honest figure is the revenue you can show, called known revenue, together with a count of the paid orders that still have no price. The figure first filters the paid orders and counts the missing price. It then totals the known revenue.

afterFigure.text: sum() skips missing values, so the total is 50.0 and order 3 adds nothing to it. The argument min_count=1 only makes sure a group where every value is missing gives a missing total and not 0. Reading 50 on its own would be a mistake, because the report must also say that one price is unknown. A reader can then decide whether 50 is close enough or whether to chase the missing price first.

unknown_prices = paid['price'].isna().sum()

steps.headline: Two paid orders sold 3 units at £4 and 2 units at £9. A third sold 5 units at an unknown price. What is the known revenue, and what must the report say?

workedSteps.text: Each order with a known price gives units times its price.
The order with the unknown price adds nothing that is known. The report must call the total known revenue and say that one price is unknown.

steps.headline: Adding a region to each order

lead.text: The last check is about a table brought in from outside. The report should show each order's region, but the order table only knows the shop. A second table, called a lookup, lists each shop once with its region. merge matches every order to the lookup row with the same shop, as it did in the lesson on combining tables.

This is safe only while each shop appears once in the lookup. If the lookup listed Bay twice, every Bay order would match both rows and turn into two rows, and a total taken afterwards would count those orders twice. Adding validate='many_to_one' makes merge stop with an error when the lookup repeats a shop. The figure merges the orders with a tidy lookup. It then removes Lake from the lookup and adds indicator=True, to show what an unmatched order looks like.

afterFigure.text: In the first case every order gets a region and the table still has 5 rows, which is what a safe merge must give. In the second, Lake's order has no match, so its region is missing and the _merge column says left_only. Two checks protect the report: the row count must not change, and unmatched rows must be looked at before anyone totals.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Lake', 'Hill'], 'units': [2, 3, 4, 1, 2], 'price': [5, 8, None, 6, 8], 'paid': [True, True, True, False, True]})
lookup = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Lake'], 'region': ['East', 'West', 'East']})
result = orders.merge(lookup, on='shop', how='left', validate='many_to_one')

lead.text: validate='many_to_one' guards the lookup. Think about what a merge should do when the guard finds a shop listed twice.
Each order is matched with every lookup row that has its shop. Count the rows the merge produces.

reveal.text: Each Bay order appeared once for every Bay record in the lookup, so the join added rows. Revenue totalled after it would have been inflated.

lead.text: Put the checks together and the report says what it can stand behind. Unpaid orders were left out first. Grouping the paid orders by shop then gives one row per shop, with the known revenue and the number of unknown prices side by side. Bay shows a known revenue of 10 and one unknown price, so its true revenue is at least 10. Hill's two orders are both priced, so its 40 is complete.
Then someone confirms that order 3 sold at £5 a unit. The gap is filled with a real value, and the figure shows the same report built again. Bay's revenue is no longer a floor.

afterFigure.text: Bay's 30 is the 10 from order 1 plus 4 × 5 = 20 from order 3. The caveat disappeared because a fact arrived, and nobody guessed. Until then, known revenue with a count of unknown prices was the honest report. The same habits cover the whole table. Check the grain and decide who counts. Say what is unknown, and count the rows after every merge.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Lake', 'Hill'], 'units': [2, 3, 4, 1, 2], 'price': [5, 8, None, 6, 8], 'paid': [True, True, True, False, True]})
paid = orders[orders['paid']].copy()
paid['revenue'] = paid['units'] * paid['price']
paid['unknown_price'] = paid['price'].isna()
result = paid.groupby('shop', as_index=False).agg(known_revenue=('revenue', lambda s: s.sum(min_count=1)), unknown_prices=('unknown_price', 'sum'))

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Lake', 'Hill'], 'units': [2, 3, 4, 1, 2], 'price': [5, 8, None, 6, 8], 'paid': [True, True, True, False, True]})
orders.loc[orders['id'] == 3, 'price'] = 5
paid = orders[orders['paid']].copy()
paid['revenue'] = paid['units'] * paid['price']
result = paid.groupby('shop', as_index=False)['revenue'].sum()

lead.text: Lake is a different shop with its own paid orders from another week. Work out its revenue the way the report did for Bay.

reveal.text: The confirmed price turns the caveat into a number. Until then the honest report was known revenue plus a count of unknown prices.

lesson.orientation: Audit grain, missing measurements and lookup keys before reporting paid revenue.
lesson.reviewLabel: Build a report you can defend
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: The sales report from the last lesson's closing note is on your desk. It lists five orders, with the shop, the units sold, the price of one unit and whether the customer has paid. The totals at the bottom look sensible, and a manager would sign it without a second glance. That is the risk with a sales report: a wrong total looks exactly like a right one.

Nothing on the page says anything is wrong. The trouble lies in what the numbers quietly assume. An order may have been entered twice. An unpaid order may have slipped into the revenue. A price that nobody recorded may have been counted as zero. A table joined on from elsewhere may have copied some orders without a word.
In this lesson you'll check the report four ways before you trust it, in the order a careful analyst would. You finish with a report you can defend when someone asks where a figure came from.

intro.promise: By the end you'll check a sales table for repeated orders, unpaid rows, missing prices and joins that copy rows.

recap.keyIdea: A defensible report checks the grain and decides who counts. It labels known revenue with its unknowns and validates every lookup before totalling.

blocks.text: You flagged 1 repeated id in a short list and kept 3 paid orders out of 4. Seven rows came out of a join with a repeated lookup key, and Lake's revenue reached £28 once its missing price was confirmed.

recap.nextHook: You can now build a report from tidy data and say what it leaves out. A table you gather yourself will have faults nobody has listed for you, and the next step is to audit one of your own.

questions.prompt: Order IDs are 1, 2, 2 and 3. How many rows does duplicated() flag?
hints: Which rows have an id that already appeared higher up the list?
The first row with each id is not flagged.
Only the later copy of the repeated id is flagged. How many are there?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the second occurrence of ID 2 is flagged with the default keep='first'.

questions.onCorrect: 1. The second occurrence of id 2 is flagged, and the first is not.

misconceptions.feedback: The first occurrence is kept unflagged by default. Only the later repeat is flagged.

questions.prompt: Paid flags are True, False, True and True. How many orders belong in the paid report?
hints: Define the population before aggregating.
The paid flag decides which rows belong.
Count the True flags.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three rows have a true paid flag.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The paid flag defines the population, and three rows have it set to True.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every order. The unpaid one is excluded.
That counts the False flag. The paid orders are the True ones.

questions.prompt: A paid order has an unknown price. Which report label preserves that limitation?
hints: Think about what a zero price would claim about the order.
The total should say which part of the picture it leaves out.
Choose the label that gives the measured amount and the count of unknowns.

acceptedIdeas: Known revenue, with the unknown-price count
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Known revenue reports the measured amount while the missing-price count states what the total excludes.

choices.label: Known revenue, with the unknown-price count
Revenue after silently replacing the price with zero

questions.onCorrect: Known revenue, with the unknown-price count. The label says what the total excludes.

misconceptions.feedback: The total is not complete while a price is unknown.
A zero price claims the order earned nothing. The data does not say that.

questions.prompt: A shop lookup contains two records for the same shop. What should a many-to-one enrichment do?
hints: Think about the relationship you expect between orders and lookup keys.
A repeated key in the lookup copies orders when the merge runs.
Choose the option that stops the problem before any total is taken.

acceptedIdeas: Reject the ambiguous lookup and resolve it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Validate the lookup before reporting. Resolve the duplicate according to its meaning rather than multiplying orders.

choices.label: Reject the ambiguous lookup and resolve it
Duplicate each order and continue silently

questions.onCorrect: Reject the ambiguous lookup and resolve it. Duplicate keys would copy orders and inflate revenue.

misconceptions.feedback: Copying orders is how revenue gets inflated, so it must not pass silently.
Throwing away every order is not needed. The lookup needs fixing.

questions.prompt: Two paid orders sold 2 units at £7 and 3 units at £5. A third sold 4 units at an unknown price. What is the known revenue, in pounds?
hints: Sum only the two known products.
The unknown-price order adds nothing known.
Work out 2 × 7 + 3 × 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known rows contribute 14 and 15, totalling 29. The unknown row remains a caveat.

questions.onCorrect: £29. The known rows give 14 and 15. The unknown row stays a caveat in the report.

misconceptions.feedback: That would price the unknown order, which nobody knows.
That is only the first order. The second is known too.

questions.prompt: Two paid orders sold 2 units at £7 and 3 units at £5. A third sold 4 units at a newly confirmed £6. What is the complete revenue, in pounds?
hints: Add the newly confirmed order.
The third order now has a price.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The confirmed order adds 4 × 6 = 24 to the known 29, producing 53.

questions.onCorrect: £53. The confirmed order adds 24 to the known 29, and nothing is left unknown.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the order whose price is now confirmed.
That is only the confirmed order. The other two count too.

hints: Which orders are paid?
Which of those have a price?
Count the orders that satisfy both.
questions.prompt: Paid flags are True, True, False and True, and prices are 5, unknown, 4 and 3. How many paid orders have a known price?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first and fourth orders are paid with known prices.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Orders 1 and 4 are paid and priced. Order 2 is paid but has no known price.

misconceptions.feedback: One of the paid orders has an unknown price.
Two paid orders have a price.

hints: Which orders count in the report?
Order B is not paid, so it is left out.
Work out 5 × 4 + 3 × 6.

questions.onCorrect: £38. The unpaid order was left out before totalling. Deciding who counts comes before any sum.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the unpaid order. Only paid orders count.

choices.label: Check that the order ids are unique
Check that the shop names are unique
Check that the prices are all different

acceptedIdeas: Check that the order ids are unique
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The id identifies an order, so it must not repeat.

questions.onCorrect: Check that the order ids are unique. A repeated id means one order may sit on two rows.

misconceptions.feedback: A shop can receive many orders, so repeated shop names are expected.
Two orders can have the same price. The id identifies the order.

Four orders, and some are in the report.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Only the unpaid order is left out of the paid report.

questions.onCorrect: 7. The two Bay orders each appeared twice, adding two rows to the original five.

hints: Work out each order's revenue from units and price.
The unknown price is now 6.
Add 2 × 5 to 3 × 6.

questions.onCorrect: £28. The confirmed price lets the second order count, giving 10 and 18.
